name: Belief perseverance
statement: A belief built on evidence that is later shown to be wholly fabricated does not return to where it started.
meaning: The claim is narrower than "people resist argument". It concerns the one case where the normative answer is not in doubt: every scrap of evidence behind a belief is revealed to the believer as invented, and the belief should therefore revert to its prior state. Anderson, Lepper and Ross set out that reasoning in 1980, noting that everyday disputes rarely permit anyone to say how much revision an attack warrants, while total discrediting does. What the experiments measure is the residue after that discrediting. Two things are being measured across the literature. One is self-perception, where false feedback on a rigged task shapes what people think of their own ability. The other is a general theory about how two variables relate, held by someone with no stake in the answer. Siebert and Siebert define the modern version as opinions that persevere after the information behind them has been retracted, and separate it from the continued influence effect, which concerns retracted facts still feeding inferential reasoning about an event.

origin.who: Lee Ross, Mark R. Lepper and Michael Hubbard
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper reported two experiments in a debriefing paradigm and concluded that process debriefing, unlike standard outcome debriefing, generally eliminated the erroneous self-perceptions. The phrase in the title is "perseverance in self-perception and social perception"; Anderson, Lepper and Ross called it theory perseverance in 1980, and Anderson used the words belief perseverance in 1983.

evidence: Ross, Lepper and Hubbard ran Experiment 1 on 60 female high school juniors and seniors recruited by newspaper advertisement for $2. Each sorted 25 pairs of suicide notes into authentic and inauthentic, and was told she had scored 24 (success), 17 (average) or 10 (failure). After a delay of 5 or 25 minutes the experimenter explained that the score had been fixed in advance. Estimates of past and future performance still tracked the discredited feedback, F(1, 54) = 16.07 for own past performance minus estimated average performance. Experiment 2 used 144 female Stanford undergraduates, 72 acting and 72 watching as yoked observers, with data from a further 24 unobserved actors set aside. Actors given no debriefing estimated 22.75 correct after success feedback and 9.50 after failure. Outcome debriefing moved those to 18.33 and 12.83. Process debriefing, which added a discussion of the perseverance mechanism itself, moved them to 16.50 and 15.17. Anderson, Lepper and Ross switched the object from self-image to a social theory. Seventy Stanford undergraduates read two case studies suggesting that risk taking either predicted or undermined success as a firefighter. Before debriefing the manipulation produced F(1, 63) = 20.21 on a composite belief measure. After subjects were told the cases were fictitious it produced F(1, 63) = 17.43, and the reduction was not statistically reliable, F(1, 63) = 1.59. Their second experiment, with 62 subjects and 60 analysed in cells of 10, found that debriefing did dampen the beliefs, interaction F(1, 54) = 23.31, while leaving them apart in both the explanation, F(1, 54) = 69.74, and no explanation, F(1, 54) = 19.24, conditions.

replication.headline: Siebert and Siebert re-ran the firefighter paradigm on 366 people and found opinions still displaced from baseline after retraction, d = 0.80.
replication.detail: The residue survives repetition, in the original paradigm and in newer ones. Anderson gave 98 undergraduates either two case histories or a statistical summary of 20 firefighters, matched for the strength of the belief they induced, and debriefed everyone. Perseverance was present at once, F(1, 90) = 28.43, and a week later, F(1, 84) = 23.53, though at a week only the case-history group still showed it. Siebert and Siebert used the same firefighter topic with a fabricated study summary and two case studies, measuring opinions before misinformation, after it, after retraction and after a debiasing treatment. Of 366 participants, 312 (85%) shifted after the misinformation and 251 (68.5%) were still displaced from their own baseline after the retraction, d = 0.80. Their 2024 study moved to a real-world topic, a fabricated blog article about remote versus in-office work, and 364 of 876 participants (42%) remained displaced after retraction, d = 0.52. Greenspan and Loftus tested the same logic on memory rather than opinion. In their Study 1, 373 participants watched a video, some received misinformation, and half were debriefed; a week later the misinformation effect was still there, at phi = .12 on one critical item and phi = .15 on the other. Miketta and Friese ran six studies in which participants received false feedback about their intelligence or their attractiveness, and report that lower well-being and more hostile attributions survived written debriefing, in-person debriefing and a self-affirming essay, with affective consequences lasting two weeks and longer. No multi-laboratory replication project has taken the effect on.

study.cite: Siebert, J., & Siebert, J. U. (2023). Effective mitigation of the belief perseverance bias after the retraction of misinformation: Awareness training and counter-speech. PLOS ONE, 18(3), e0282202.

limits: The mechanism has held up worse than the effect. Anderson, Lepper and Ross attributed perseverance to the causal explanations people build, reporting a point-biserial correlation of .44 between the presence of a general explanatory principle in a subject's writing and the size of the residue. Anderson's own 1983 study then asked half its subjects to write explanations and found no effect of doing so in either session, F values below 1, which he described as contrary to previous findings. The effect is also not irreversible, and every study that has tried a better debriefing has moved it. Ross, Lepper and Hubbard's process debriefing nearly closed the gap in 1975. Greenspan and Loftus wrote an enhanced debriefing that named the misinformation and explained how memory errors arise, and in their Study 2, with 439 participants, it removed the effect on one critical item. Siebert and Siebert found counter-speech returned opinions to baseline, with the difference between initial and post-treatment opinion at 0.12 on a seven-point scale and not statistically reliable. Anglin, Rath, Yuodsnukis and Miller report three preregistered experiments on capital punishment, gun control, and video games and aggression in which participants shifted their beliefs towards disconfirming evidence and held the shift a day later, which is the opposite paradigm and the opposite result. No meta-analysis of belief perseverance was located; searches of Crossref, PubMed and the open web returned meta-analyses of debunking and of the continued influence effect, not of this literature. McFarland, Cheam and Buehler's direct replication and extension of the debriefing paradigm sits behind a paywall and could not be read for this entry. The two 1975 experiments used only female participants, and both 1980 experiments used Stanford undergraduates in cells of about ten.
misreadings: Belief perseverance is not the continued influence effect, and Siebert and Siebert draw the line by paradigm. Belief perseverance gives people information on a topic, retracts it, then asks their opinion on the topic. The continued influence paradigm gives people pieces of a developing event, retracts one, then asks open-ended inference questions and watches them reach for the retracted piece. Greenspan and Loftus note that the two names are applied to closely related procedures, so the boundary is a matter of what is measured rather than a difference in kind. Neither is the backfire effect, which requires the correction to push belief further in the wrong direction; perseverance means the correction does less than it should, not less than nothing. The line most often overstated is that debriefing does not work. Ross, Lepper and Hubbard's own abstract says process debriefing generally eliminated the erroneous self-perceptions, and their conclusion was addressed to the ethics of deception research rather than to human stubbornness in general. Greenspan and Loftus are a caution in the other direction: their enhanced debriefing wiped out the effect on the question about what was stolen, chi-square 0.28 with 439 participants, and left it intact on the question about the jacket, phi = .17.
